noteBlocks.lede: Your body fights microorganisms in three ways: it keeps them out, it engulfs the ones that get in, and it makes antibodies that fit one kind exactly. It also remembers, which is why the same illness rarely strikes twice. Nearly every mark here is a precise word.
can: Name the barriers and describe how blood clots at a cut.
Explain how antibodies fit antigens, clump microorganisms, and how phagocytes finish the job.
Explain the faster second response with memory lymphocytes, and tell active from passive immunity.

noteBlocks.caption: Three lines of defence: keep microorganisms out, engulf the ones that get in, and target one kind with antibodies.

noteBlocks.md: The first line of defence stops microorganisms getting in at all. The **skin** is a **barrier** they cannot cross. **Mucous membranes** line the nose and airways: their sticky mucus **traps** microorganisms, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it to the throat to be swallowed.

noteBlocks.caption: A clot seals a cut: fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, and a scab forms on top.

noteBlocks.md: A cut opens a gap, so **blood clotting** closes it. The plasma carries a protein, **fibrinogen**, dissolved in it. At a cut, **platelets** set off its change into **fibrin**, which is not soluble: long threads that tangle into a mesh.

noteBlocks.stem: A cook cuts a finger while chopping onions. Describe how a clot forms at the cut. [3]

steps.working: Platelets at the cut cause soluble fibrinogen in the plasma to change into insoluble fibrin.
steps.decision: Start at the cut with the platelets: they begin the change, and the protein's two names are the first mark.

steps.working: The fibrin threads form a mesh that traps red blood cells, making a clot.
steps.decision: Say what the threads do: a mesh that catches cells is the clot itself.

steps.working: The clot dries into a scab, which stops blood loss and keeps microorganisms out.
steps.decision: Finish with what the clot is for: both jobs, blood in and microorganisms out.

noteBlocks.prompt: A medicine stops fibrinogen from changing into fibrin. What happens when someone taking it cuts a finger?
options: the blood does not clot, so the bleeding goes on longer
the cut clots faster than usual
no white blood cells reach the cut
noteBlocks.answer: the blood does not clot, so the bleeding goes on longer
noteBlocks.explain: Steps 1 and 2 of the See it: fibrinogen must become fibrin, whose threads make the mesh that traps blood cells. Stop that change and no mesh forms, so no clot: the bleeding goes on longer.

optionNotes.option: the cut clots faster than usual
optionNotes.why: Without fibrin there are no threads to make a mesh, so a clot cannot form at all, let alone faster.

optionNotes.option: no white blood cells reach the cut
optionNotes.why: The medicine does not touch white blood cells; what fails is the fibrin mesh that makes the clot.

twin.prompt: A person's plasma has almost no fibrinogen. What happens at a cut?
options: no fibrin mesh forms, so the blood does not clot
the platelets make antibodies instead
the skin grows over the cut at once
twin.answer: no fibrin mesh forms, so the blood does not clot
twin.explain: Fibrin is made from fibrinogen; with almost none there is nothing to make the threads, so no mesh and no clot. Platelets make no antibodies.

noteBlocks.caption: The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen's shape, so the two fit together.

noteBlocks.md: A microorganism that gets past the barriers carries molecules on its surface called **antigens**, and each kind has its own shape. White blood cells called **lymphocytes** respond by making **antibodies** whose shape is **complementary** to that antigen: the reverse of it, so the two fit like a key in its lock.

noteBlocks.title: Why one antibody fits one microorganism
noteBlocks.md: A complementary shape fits one antigen only, so a new microorganism needs new antibodies, and making them takes several days. The shapes are never the same: a copy of the antigen's shape could not fit over it.

noteBlocks.stem: A child's lymphocytes have made antibodies against the measles virus. Explain why these antibodies do not attach to a chickenpox virus. [2]

steps.working: Each antibody has a shape that is complementary to the antigen on the measles virus.
steps.decision: Name the shape word the marks want, complementary, and what it matches: the antigen, not the whole virus.

steps.working: The chickenpox virus carries antigens of a different shape, so the antibody does not fit them.
steps.decision: Then compare: a different antigen shape means no fit, so no attachment.

noteBlocks.prompt: How does the shape of an antibody compare with the shape of the antigen it attaches to?
options: it is complementary to the antigen
it is the same shape as the antigen
it matches the whole microorganism
noteBlocks.answer: it is complementary to the antigen
noteBlocks.explain: This is step 1 of the See it. The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen, a socket its point slides into, not a copy of it. And it fits the antigen on the surface, not the whole microorganism. The word is complementary.

optionNotes.option: it is the same shape as the antigen
optionNotes.why: It sounds right because the two fit, but a copy of the antigen's shape could not slide over it: the antibody is its reverse.
The antibody fits one small molecule on the surface, the antigen, not the outline of the whole microorganism.

twin.prompt: An antibody attaches to a bacterium. Which part of the bacterium does its shape fit?
options: an antigen on its surface
the whole bacterium
the bacterium's cell wall
twin.explain: Antibodies are made against antigens, the molecules on a microorganism's surface, and fit those alone: complementary to the antigen, not to the whole cell.

noteBlocks.caption: Antibodies hold microorganisms together in a clump; a phagocyte then engulfs the clump and digests it.

noteBlocks.md: An antibody has more than one tip, so it can hold two microorganisms at once. Thousands do this and **clump** them together. Stuck in a clump, they cannot spread or reproduce, so there are fewer to cause symptoms. A different white blood cell, a **phagocyte**, then **engulfs** the clump and **digests** it.

noteBlocks.title: Three words, three marks
noteBlocks.md: The Summer 2024 report wanted the standard terms here: name the phagocyte, say it engulfs, say it digests. 'The white blood cells eat them' names none of the three.

noteBlocks.stem: A splinter carries bacteria into a finger, and antibodies attach to them. Describe how the bacteria are then destroyed. [4]

steps.working: The antibodies clump the bacteria together.
steps.decision: Start where the stem leaves off: attached antibodies hold the bacteria in clumps.

steps.working: Clumped bacteria cannot spread or reproduce.
steps.decision: Say what clumping achieves before anything destroys them.

steps.working: A phagocyte engulfs a clump, surrounding it.
steps.decision: Name the cell and the verb: phagocyte, engulfs.

steps.working: The phagocyte digests the bacteria inside it.
steps.decision: The last word the marks want: digests.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Immune System"
noteBlocks.why: Phagocytes, lymphocytes and antibodies, made for another exam board: it adds antitoxins, which CCEA does not examine, and leaves out active and passive immunity, which it does.

noteBlocks.prompt: A phagocyte reaches a clump of bacteria held together by antibodies. In what order does it deal with them?
options: it engulfs the clump, then digests the bacteria
it digests the bacteria, then engulfs the clump
it makes antibodies, then engulfs the clump
noteBlocks.answer: it engulfs the clump, then digests the bacteria
noteBlocks.explain: Steps 3 and 4 of the See it: the phagocyte first engulfs the clump, surrounding it, and only then digests the bacteria inside. It cannot digest what it has not taken in, and antibodies come from lymphocytes.

optionNotes.option: it digests the bacteria, then engulfs the clump
optionNotes.why: Both verbs are right but the order is reversed: the clump has to be inside the phagocyte before it can be digested.

optionNotes.option: it makes antibodies, then engulfs the clump
optionNotes.why: Making antibodies is the lymphocytes' job, and it happened before the clump formed; the phagocyte's own steps are engulf, then digest.

twin.prompt: A phagocyte has just engulfed a clump of viruses. What does it do next?
options: it digests the viruses inside it
it makes antibodies against them
it releases the clump unharmed
twin.answer: it digests the viruses inside it
twin.explain: Engulfing comes first and digesting second: once the clump is inside, the phagocyte digests the viruses. Making antibodies is the lymphocytes' job.

noteBlocks.text: 4. Two white blood cells, two jobs

noteBlocks.md: Two kinds of white blood cell share the work, and the marks depend on keeping them apart. **Lymphocytes** make antibodies, each against one antigen. **Phagocytes** engulf and digest. Platelets are not white blood cells at all: they start clotting.

noteBlocks.stem: A blood test counts two kinds of white blood cell. State what each kind does when bacteria get into the body. [2]

steps.working: Lymphocytes make antibodies against the bacteria's antigens.
steps.decision: One cell, one job: say which chemical lymphocytes make.

steps.working: Phagocytes engulf the bacteria and digest them.
steps.decision: The other cell, the other job: the two verbs of phagocytosis.

noteBlocks.prompt: A child is born with very few lymphocytes but a normal number of phagocytes. Which of her defences is weakest?
options: making antibodies against a new microorganism
engulfing and digesting microorganisms
forming a clot at a cut
noteBlocks.answer: making antibodies against a new microorganism
noteBlocks.explain: Step 1 of the See it: lymphocytes are the cells that make antibodies. With few of them, antibodies against a new microorganism come slowly or not at all; her phagocytes still engulf and digest, and platelets still clot her blood.

optionNotes.why: That is the phagocytes' job, and her phagocytes are normal; what the missing lymphocytes do is make antibodies.

optionNotes.option: forming a clot at a cut
optionNotes.why: Clotting is started by platelets, which are not white blood cells, so having few lymphocytes leaves it unchanged.

twin.prompt: An adult has very few phagocytes but a normal number of lymphocytes. Which of his defences is weakest?
options: engulfing and digesting microorganisms
making antibodies against a new microorganism
forming a clot at a cut
twin.explain: Phagocytes engulf and digest, so with few of them that defence is weakest; his lymphocytes can still make antibodies, and platelets still start clots.

noteBlocks.alt: A graph of antibody concentration against time. After the first exposure, on day 0, antibodies appear on day 5 and rise slowly to a small peak of 25 units on day 12. After a second exposure to the same antigen, on day 35, antibodies appear on day 37 and rise fast to a peak of 75 units on day 41.
noteBlocks.caption: After the second exposure to the same antigen, antibodies appear sooner and reach a far higher level.

noteBlocks.md: The first time a microorganism gets in, making the right antibodies takes days, and you may feel ill meanwhile. Some of the lymphocytes then stay in the blood as **memory lymphocytes**. If the same microorganism returns, they recognise its antigen at once, and antibodies are made faster, in greater numbers, and last longer.

noteBlocks.stem: The graph shows one person's antibody concentration after two exposures to the same microorganism. Compare the two responses.

steps.working: First exposure: antibodies appear after 5 days and peak at 25 units.
steps.decision: Read the first hump: when the line leaves the axis, then its top against the grid.

steps.working: Second exposure, on day 35: antibodies appear after 2 days and peak at 75 units.
steps.decision: Count the days from the second exposure, day 35, not from day 0.

steps.working: 75 ÷ 25 = 3: the second response is faster, 3 times larger, and lasts longer.
steps.decision: How many times greater means divide the larger peak by the smaller, never subtract.

noteBlocks.prompt: On another person's antibody graph, the first peak is 15 units and the peak after a second exposure to the same antigen is 75 units. How many times greater is the second peak?
noteBlocks.explain: This is step 3 of the See it. "How many times greater" asks for a division, the larger peak over the smaller, not a subtraction: 75 ÷ 15 = 5 times greater.

twin.prompt: A first antibody peak is 18 units, and the peak after a second exposure to the same antigen is 72 units. How many times greater is the second peak?
twin.explain: Divide the larger peak by the smaller: 72 ÷ 18 = 4 times greater. Subtracting would give how many units higher, which is not what is asked.

noteBlocks.md: Ask one question: did your own lymphocytes make the antibodies? If yes, after an infection or a vaccine, it is **active immunity**, and it lasts because memory lymphocytes remain. If the antibodies arrived ready-made, across the placenta before birth, in a mother's milk or by injection, it is **passive immunity**.

Passive immunity works at once but fades: the antibodies are broken down, nothing replaces them, and no memory lymphocytes were made. A graph shows it as a falling line against the level needed for immunity.

noteBlocks.stem: A patient is injected with antibodies on day 0 at 96 units. The graph shows the level falling; 24 units are needed for immunity. For how long is the patient immune, and why does it end?

steps.working: Immune from day 0: the level starts at 96 units, above the 24 needed.
steps.decision: Ready-made antibodies protect at once: no days of waiting as there are when lymphocytes must make them.

steps.working: The curve crosses the dashed line at 24 units on day 16, the last day of immunity.
steps.decision: Read along the level needed to where the curve meets it, then down to the days.

steps.working: It ends because the injected antibodies are broken down and no memory lymphocytes were made: passive immunity.
steps.decision: Name the type from who made the antibodies: not her lymphocytes, so passive.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these gives a person active immunity?
options: a tetanus vaccination
antibodies in breast milk
an injection of ready-made antibodies
noteBlocks.explain: Ask the See it's question: who made the antibodies? After a vaccination her own lymphocytes make them, so the immunity is active and it lasts. Milk and an injection bring ready-made antibodies: passive, as in step 3.

optionNotes.why: The baby is protected, but its own lymphocytes made nothing: antibodies that arrive ready-made give passive immunity.
This is the See it's case: the antibodies arrive ready-made and are broken down, so the immunity is passive, not active.

twin.prompt: Which of these gives a newborn baby passive immunity?
options: antibodies in its mother's milk
a vaccination at two months old
recovering from an infection
twin.explain: Passive means the antibodies arrive ready-made, and milk brings them. A vaccination or an infection makes the baby's own lymphocytes produce antibodies, which is active immunity.

**Read the level needed** (2021): a line on the graph marks the level needed for immunity, so read the first and last days the curve is above it. **Why no symptoms the second time?** (2025): the marks go to memory lymphocytes and what they do, not to antibodies being specific.

noteBlocks.stem: Marking two answers to 'Explain why a person infected a second time by the same bacterium has no symptoms. [3]'. X: 'The antibodies are specific to that bacterium.' Y: 'Memory lymphocytes recognise it, so antibodies are made faster and in greater numbers.'

steps.working: X: 0 marks. Every antibody is specific, the first time too, so it explains nothing new.
steps.decision: Ask of each line: what is different the second time? The 2025 report found this answer often.

steps.working: Y: memory lymphocytes recognise the bacterium.
steps.decision: The difference is in the blood: cells kept from the first infection.

steps.working: Y: antibodies are made faster, and in greater numbers.
steps.decision: Two more points: how soon and how many, so the bacteria are destroyed before symptoms.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question asks why a person infected a second time with the same bacterium has no symptoms. Which answer earns the marks?
options: memory lymphocytes make antibodies faster and in greater numbers
the antibodies are specific to that bacterium
the bacterium is weaker the second time
noteBlocks.answer: memory lymphocytes make antibodies faster and in greater numbers
noteBlocks.explain: This is answer Y in the See it. The question is about what is different the second time: being specific is true the first time too, and the bacterium is the same. The memory lymphocytes are new, so antibodies come faster and in greater numbers.

optionNotes.option: the antibodies are specific to that bacterium
optionNotes.why: True of every antibody, the first time as well, so it explains nothing new; the 2025 report found this answer often.

optionNotes.option: the bacterium is weaker the second time
optionNotes.why: The bacterium is the same both times; what has changed is the blood, which now holds memory lymphocytes.

twin.prompt: A student explains why a vaccinated person does not fall ill when infected. Which line earns a mark?
options: memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once
antibodies are specific to one antigen
the vaccine kills the microorganism
twin.answer: memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once
twin.explain: The vaccine left memory lymphocytes, which is what differs when the real microorganism arrives. Being specific is true of all antibodies, and a vaccine does not kill the microorganism.

noteBlocks.md:
Name the barriers, **skin**, **mucous membranes** and **blood clotting**, and describe how a clot forms.
Explain that **lymphocytes** make **antibodies** complementary to one **antigen**.
Describe clumping, then a **phagocyte** that engulfs and digests.
Explain the faster, larger second response with **memory lymphocytes**, and tell **active** from **passive** immunity.

Expect a short question on both tiers: barriers to name, an antibody to choose or explain, what happens after clumping, or why the second response is different. The marks are nearly all words: complementary, antigen, phagocyte, engulf, digest, memory lymphocytes. Stuck? Write the steps in order, one short sentence each.

workedExamples.stem: Years after recovering from measles, a woman is exposed to the measles virus again. She does not become ill. Explain why. [3]

steps.working: Memory lymphocytes made during her first infection are still in her blood.
steps.decision: Start with what is different this time: the memory lymphocytes left from the first infection.

options: Because the second response depends on cells left from the first
Because the virus is weaker the second time
Because antibodies are specific
whyMenu.explain: The virus is the same; what has changed is her blood, which now holds memory lymphocytes. Every antibody is specific, so that explains nothing new.

steps.working: They recognise the virus's antigen, so antibodies are made much faster.
steps.decision: Say how soon: the first mark of the difference.

steps.working: Far more antibodies are made, so the virus is destroyed before she has symptoms.
steps.decision: Say how many, and link it to no illness.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Memory lymphocytes from her first infection recognise the antigen, so antibodies are made faster and in greater numbers, and the virus is destroyed before she has symptoms.

steps.working: First peak: 20 units
steps.decision: Read the top of the first hump against the grid.

steps.working: Second peak: 160 units
steps.decision: Read the top of the second hump the same way.

options: Times greater asks for a ratio, so divide
Subtract to find how much higher
Add the two peaks

items.stem: Before the lesson, three things from earlier topics; nobody expects you to know this lesson yet. Which blood cells fight infection?
items.skill: Recall the job of white blood cells

options.feedback: White blood cells. This lesson is about the two kinds and what each does.
Red blood cells carry oxygen.
Platelets help blood clot. That is a defence too, but it is not how infection is fought.
Plasma is the liquid that carries the cells.
A microorganism, such as a bacterium or a virus, that causes disease.
That is an antibiotic.
White blood cells fight pathogens.
A pathogen comes from outside the body.

options.text: they help the blood to clot
options.feedback: They start clotting at a cut.
That is red blood cells.
That is lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell.
That is plasma.

items.stem: How does an antibody's shape compare with the shape of its antigen?

options.text: it is complementary to the antigen
options.feedback: Complementary: the reverse of the antigen, so it fits that antigen only.

options.text: it is the same shape as the antigen
options.feedback: The same shape could not fit over it. The Summer 2024 report found this slip often.
It fits the antigen on the microorganism's surface, not the microorganism.
Each antibody has one shape, made for one antigen.

items.stem: What does a phagocyte do to a microorganism?

options.feedback: Engulf, then digest: the words the scheme uses.
That is a lymphocyte.
Antibodies clump microorganisms; phagocytes then engulf the clump.

options.text: turns it into a memory cell
options.feedback: Memory lymphocytes come from lymphocytes, not from microorganisms.

items.stem: Why is the second response to the same microorganism faster?

options.text: memory lymphocytes from the first infection are already there
options.feedback: Memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once, so antibodies come faster and in greater numbers.

options.text: the antibodies are specific to the microorganism
options.feedback: Every antibody is specific; that is not what is different the second time. The Summer 2025 report found answers like this.

options.text: the microorganism is weaker the second time
options.feedback: The microorganism is the same; the body is ready for it.

options.text: phagocytes make antibodies the second time
options.feedback: Phagocytes never make antibodies.

items.stem: A baby is born with antibodies that crossed the placenta from its mother. What type of immunity is this?

options.feedback: Passive: the antibodies arrived ready-made, so they do not last.
Active immunity is when your own lymphocytes make the antibodies.
Memory lymphocytes are part of active immunity; none were made here.
The antibodies do protect the baby, for a while.

items.stem: Which structures keep microorganisms out of the body in the first place?

options.text: skin, mucous membranes and blood clots
options.feedback: The three barriers the specification names.
These act once microorganisms are inside.
Red blood cells carry oxygen.
These act once microorganisms are inside, on a second infection.

context.setting: A graze, a runny nose and unbroken skin: the barriers at work

parts.stem: A graze on a knee is covered by a scab within minutes. Name the process in the blood that makes the scab.
hints: The blood at the graze turns from a liquid into a solid plug.
parts.workedSolution: Blood clotting.

parts.stem: The lining of the nose makes mucus. Explain how the mucus helps to stop microorganisms reaching the lungs.

accepted: the mucus is sticky, so it traps microorganisms

scheme.for: it is sticky and traps (catches) microorganisms

hints: What happens to a small thing that lands on something sticky?
parts.workedSolution: The mucus is sticky, so it traps microorganisms before they reach the lungs.

parts.stem: State how unbroken skin protects the body from microorganisms.

accepted: it is a barrier that microorganisms cannot get through

scheme.for: it is a (physical) barrier: microorganisms cannot get through it

hints: Think of the skin as a layer between the outside and your blood.
parts.workedSolution: It is a barrier: microorganisms cannot get through unbroken skin.

context.setting: Which cell does which job, and one sentence to put right

parts.stem: Which type of white blood cell surrounds microorganisms and breaks them down?
hints: Its name means a cell that eats.
parts.workedSolution: Phagocytes.

parts.stem: A student writes: 'Phagocytes make antibiotics that attach to the antigens.' Two of the words are wrong. Write the sentence correctly.

accepted: lymphocytes make antibodies that attach to the antigens

hints: Which white blood cells make the chemicals that attach to antigens?
Antibiotics are medicines; what does the body make?
parts.workedSolution: Lymphocytes make antibodies that attach to the antigens.

context.setting: A person whose phagocytes engulf bacteria but cannot digest them

parts.stem: In a rare condition, a person's phagocytes can engulf bacteria but cannot digest them. Their lymphocytes work normally. Bacteria get into a cut in this person's skin. Describe what happens to the bacteria, and suggest why the infection lasts longer than usual.

accepted: lymphocytes make antibodies that attach to the antigens and clump the bacteria together; phagocytes engulf the clumps but cannot digest them, so the bacteria are not destroyed

scheme.for: lymphocytes make antibodies (against the bacteria's antigens)
the antibodies clump the bacteria together
but cannot digest them, so the bacteria are not destroyed (survive), and the infection lasts
scheme.examinerNote: The first three marks are the sequence the specification names; the fourth applies it: engulfing without digesting does not destroy the bacteria.

hints: Run the usual sequence: which steps still work?
What does engulfing alone fail to do?
parts.workedSolution: Lymphocytes make antibodies that attach to the bacteria's antigens and clump the bacteria together. Phagocytes engulf the clumps but cannot digest them, so the bacteria are not destroyed and the infection lasts longer.

commonErrors.feedback: The shapes are not the same: they are complementary, like a key and its lock. The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen's shape, so it fits that antigen only. The Summer 2024 report found this slip often.

context.setting: Why an antibody attaches to one microorganism only

parts.stem: Lymphocytes produce antibodies against one type of microorganism. Explain why these antibodies attach only to that type of microorganism.

accepted: the antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen on that microorganism

scheme.examinerNote: The shape is complementary, not the same, and it fits the antigen, not the microorganism as a whole: the two slips the Summer 2024 report names.

hints: Compare the shape of the antibody's tip with the shape of the antigen.
Name the part of the microorganism it fits.
parts.workedSolution: The antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen on that microorganism, so it fits that antigen and no other.

commonErrors.feedback: The shapes are not the same: they are complementary, like a key and its lock. The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen's shape, so it fits that antigen only. The Summer 2024 report found this slip often.

context.setting: What happens after antibodies clump microorganisms together

parts.stem: Antibodies clump microorganisms together so that they cannot move. Suggest how this helps the body to defend itself.

accepted: the microorganisms cannot spread or reproduce

scheme.for: stops the microorganisms spreading or reproducing (so fewer symptoms)

hints: What can a microorganism no longer do once it is stuck in a clump?
parts.workedSolution: The microorganisms cannot spread through the body or reproduce, so there are fewer of them to cause symptoms.

parts.stem: Another kind of white blood cell then destroys the clump. Name it, and describe how it deals with the clump.

accepted: a phagocyte engulfs the clump and digests it

scheme.examinerNote: The Summer 2024 report wanted the standard terms for phagocytosis: the marks are for phagocyte, engulf and digest.

hints: Three words carry the three marks.
parts.workedSolution: A phagocyte engulfs the clump and then digests it.

commonErrors.feedback: Use the words the mark scheme uses: a phagocyte engulfs the clump, surrounding it, and then digests it. 'Eats' or 'attacks' names neither step.

context.setting: How the second response to the same microorganism differs from the first

parts.stem: A hospital measured a patient's antibody levels through two infections by the same bacterium, a year apart. Describe three ways in which her antibody levels during the second infection would be different.

accepted: antibodies are produced faster, more antibodies are produced, and they stay in the blood for longer

scheme.for: more antibodies are produced (a higher level)
they remain in the blood for longer

hints: Three differences: how soon, how many, how long.
parts.workedSolution: Antibodies are produced faster, more antibodies are produced, and they stay in the blood for longer.

context.setting: Reading the antibody graph after two exposures

figures.alt: A graph of antibody concentration against time in days, with a grid. The first exposure to a microorganism is on day 0 and a second exposure to the same microorganism on day 35; a small, slow rise follows the first and a large, fast rise follows the second.

parts.stem: Use the graph. How many days after the first exposure did antibodies first appear?
hints: Find where the line first leaves the axis after day 0.
parts.workedSolution: Antibodies first appear on day 6, 6 days after the exposure on day 0.

parts.stem: How many days after the second exposure, on day 35, did antibodies start to rise?
hints: Count the days from day 35, not from day 0.
parts.workedSolution: They start to rise on day 37: 37 − 35 = 2 days.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the day printed on the axis. The question asks how many days after the second exposure, so count from day 35.

parts.stem: Calculate how many times greater the peak antibody concentration is after the second exposure than after the first.
hints: Read both peaks from the grid, then divide the larger by the smaller.
parts.workedSolution: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 times greater.

commonErrors.feedback: That is how many units higher the second peak is. "How many times greater" means divide: 120 ÷ 20.
That divides the smaller peak by the larger, so the answer is less than 1. Put the larger peak on top.

context.setting: Sorting four cases into active and passive immunity

parts.stem: A child catches chickenpox and makes antibodies against it. State whether this gives active or passive immunity.
hints: Ask: did this person's own lymphocytes make the antibodies?
parts.workedSolution: Active: the body made its own antibodies, and memory lymphocytes.

parts.stem: A newborn baby receives antibodies in its mother's milk. State whether this gives active or passive immunity.
hints: Ask: did this person's own lymphocytes make the antibodies?
parts.workedSolution: Passive: the antibodies arrived ready-made, so no memory lymphocytes.

parts.stem: A teenager is given a vaccine and makes antibodies against it. State whether this gives active or passive immunity.
hints: Ask: did this person's own lymphocytes make the antibodies?
parts.workedSolution: Active: the body made its own antibodies, and memory lymphocytes.

parts.stem: A walker bitten by a snake is injected with antibodies against its venom. State whether this gives active or passive immunity.
hints: Ask: did this person's own lymphocytes make the antibodies?
parts.workedSolution: Passive: the antibodies arrived ready-made, so no memory lymphocytes.

parts.stem: Two brothers catch the same bacterial infection at school. Ravi had it three years ago and this time does not feel ill at all; Dev has never had it and is off school for a week. Explain why Ravi has no symptoms.

more antibodies are produced (or they last longer; she is immune), so the bacteria are destroyed before symptoms appear

parts.stem: The diagram shows a microorganism and three antibodies, A, B and C. Which antibody would lymphocytes produce against this microorganism?

options.feedback: A: its sockets are the reverse of the square antigen, so the shapes are complementary and it fits.
B's sockets are round, so they do not fit a square antigen. Look for the socket that is the reverse of the antigen.
C's tips are the same shape as the antigen, so they cannot fit over it. An antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen, the reverse of it.

hints: Find the tip that the antigen would slot into.
parts.workedSolution: A.

parts.stem: Explain your choice.

accepted: A has a shape that is complementary to the antigen

hints: Name the shape relationship and the part of the microorganism.
parts.workedSolution: A has a shape that is complementary to the antigen, so it fits it.

commonErrors.feedback: The shapes are not the same: they are complementary, like a key and its lock. The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen's shape, so it fits that antigen only. The Summer 2024 report found this slip often.

parts.stem: Describe what happens after the antibodies attach to the microorganisms.

accepted: the antibodies clump the microorganisms together so they cannot spread or reproduce, and phagocytes engulf and digest them

scheme.for: so they cannot move, spread or reproduce

hints: Three steps: clump, stop, destroy.
parts.workedSolution: The antibodies clump the microorganisms together so they cannot spread or reproduce, and phagocytes engulf and digest them.

commonErrors.feedback: Use the words the mark scheme uses: a phagocyte engulfs the clump, surrounding it, and then digests it. 'Eats' or 'attacks' names neither step.

context.setting: How blood clots at a cut, and how that defends the body

parts.stem:
Describe how blood clots when the skin is cut, and explain how clotting helps to defend the body.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: platelets at the cut start the clotting
platelets turn fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads
the mesh traps red blood cells
a clot forms, which dries into a scab
the clot seals the wound, so microorganisms cannot enter

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Seven creditworthy points in two halves, as CCEA sets this question: the process (platelets; insoluble fibrin; a mesh; trapping blood cells; a clot or scab) and the defence (stopping blood loss; keeping microorganisms out). An answer that describes the clot but never says what it keeps out has not answered the second half and should not reach the top band.

hints: Describe first: platelets, fibrin, mesh, trapped cells, clot, scab.
Then explain: what does the clot stop, and what does it keep out?
parts.workedSolution: When the skin is cut, platelets in the blood start the clotting process: they convert fibrinogen, a protein in the plasma, into insoluble fibrin threads, which form a mesh across the wound. The mesh traps red blood cells, and a clot forms, which dries to a scab. The clot stops blood loss, and it seals the cut so that microorganisms cannot enter the body.

context.setting: A doctor's record of one boy's two infections

parts.stem: A boy was infected twice by the same type of bacterium. After the first infection his antibodies took 7 days to appear and reached a peak of 30 units. After the second, they took 3 days and reached 210 units. Calculate how many times greater the second peak was.
hints: How many times greater: divide.
parts.workedSolution: 210 ÷ 30 = 7 times greater.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the difference in units. "How many times greater" means divide: 210 ÷ 30.
That divides the smaller peak by the larger. Put the larger peak on top.

parts.stem: Explain why the second response was faster and larger.

accepted: memory lymphocytes from the first infection recognised the bacteria, so antibodies were made faster and in greater numbers, and lasted longer

scheme.for: memory lymphocytes from the first infection remained (and recognised the antigen)
and more antibodies were made (they lasted longer)

hints: What was left in his blood after the first infection?
parts.workedSolution: Memory lymphocytes from the first infection recognised the bacteria, so antibodies were made faster and in greater numbers, and lasted longer.

commonErrors.feedback: That describes what every antibody is like, specific, not what is different the second time. The second response is faster and larger because memory lymphocytes from the first infection are still in the blood. The Summer 2025 report found answers like this one.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife explains why an antibody attaches to only one type of microorganism, one mark a line. Her answer:
studentWorking: The antibody is made by a lymphocyte.
The antibody has the same shape as the antigen, so it fits it.
So it attaches only to microorganisms with that antigen.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 says the same shape. An antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen, the reverse of it, which is why it fits.
correction: The antibody is made by a lymphocyte.
The antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen, so it fits it.
So it attaches only to microorganisms with that antigen.
findTheMistake.feedback: The Summer 2024 report found many answers saying the shapes were the same. Write complementary, and name the antigen.

findTheMistake.stem: Callum explains why a person infected a second time with the same bacterium has no symptoms. His answer:
studentWorking: The first infection made the person ill.
The antibodies are specific to that bacterium, so it cannot harm them.
So the second time they have no symptoms.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 describes what every antibody is like, not the secondary response. What is new is the memory lymphocytes, which make antibodies faster and in greater numbers.
correction: The first infection made the person ill.
Memory lymphocytes make antibodies faster and in greater numbers.
So the second time they have no symptoms.
findTheMistake.feedback: The Summer 2025 report found answers focused on the antibodies being specific instead of on the secondary response.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruth describes how a clump of microorganisms is destroyed. Her answer:
studentWorking: Then the white blood cells eat the clump.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 uses none of the words the marks are for. Name the cell, a phagocyte, and say what it does: it engulfs the clump and digests it.
correction: Then phagocytes engulf the clump and digest it.
findTheMistake.feedback: The Summer 2024 report asked candidates to use the normal words: phagocyte, engulf, digest.

prompts.prompt: Name the three barriers that keep microorganisms out of the body.
prompts.answer: Skin, mucous membranes and blood clotting.

prompts.prompt: What do lymphocytes make, and in response to what?
prompts.answer: Antibodies, in response to antigens on a microorganism.

prompts.prompt: How does an antibody's shape compare with its antigen's?
prompts.answer: It is complementary: the reverse of the antigen's shape, so it fits that antigen only.

prompts.prompt: How does clumping help to defend the body?
prompts.answer: Clumped microorganisms cannot move, spread or reproduce, and phagocytes can engulf them.

prompts.prompt: Why is the second response to the same microorganism faster and larger?
prompts.answer: Memory lymphocytes from the first infection recognise it and make antibodies faster and in greater numbers.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
prompts.answer: Active: your own lymphocytes make the antibodies. Passive: antibodies arrive ready-made and soon disappear.
They engulf microorganisms and digest them.

findings.asked: Identify the antibody, describe how it matches the antigen, explain immobilisation, then describe phagocytosis.
findings.wentWrong: Identifying it was easy; describing the match was not - 'the same shape' instead of complementary, and fitting 'the microorganism' rather than its antigen. Immobilisation answers were vague, and phagocytosis descriptions wandered instead of using the three expected words.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Said the antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen, that clumping stops the microorganisms reproducing or spreading, and that phagocytes engulf and digest the clump.
findings.rule: Complementary, not the same; antigen, not microorganism; phagocyte, engulf, digest.

findings.asked: The same antibody question at Foundation.
findings.wentWrong: Same pattern: the complementary idea was the sticking point and phagocytosis lacked the standard vocabulary.
findings.rule: Use the textbook words; they are the mark scheme.

findings.asked: Choose which antibody would be produced against a drawn microorganism.
findings.wentWrong: Many did not choose the antibody whose shape was complementary to the drawn antigen, though most still scored well on the rest of the question.
findings.rule: Match the antibody to the antigen's shape like a lock and key.

insight.ruleToRemember: Antigens are on the surface of the microorganism; lymphocytes make antibodies whose shape is complementary to that antigen; the antibodies bind and clump (immobilise) the microorganisms, which phagocytes then engulf and digest.
insight.aStarSignal: Choosing the right antibody from shapes and then explaining the whole sequence in the scheme's own vocabulary.
